passage: Baljeet, don't wait for me at four. I'm not coming to the auditions. No, listen. You know me: Lokesh and a stage don't mix. I already know how it goes. I walk on, my voice cracks on the first high note like it did in Class 8, the music teacher writes something on her clipboard, and the seniors in the back row smirk. Done. I can see it as clearly as I can see you. So why stand there and make it official? I'd rather keep my Saturday. You go. You'll get in, you always do. And don't say 'you never know', because I do know. That's the whole point. I'll be at home. Message me the list when it's up and I'll pretend to be happy for everyone. Actually, don't. Just tell me if you got in.

qa.q: What time was Baljeet going to wait for Lokesh?
qa.a: Baljeet was going to wait at four.

qa.q: Why does Lokesh feel so certain about how the audition would go?
qa.a: Lokesh is afraid of being embarrassed again and replays the Class 8 voice crack so vividly that the forecast feels like a memory; staying home spares Lokesh a real no.

qa.q: What small choice could give Lokesh a real answer instead of a forecast?
qa.a: Lokesh could go and sing just the first verse, treating 'I'll fail' as a guess to check, since skipping makes it impossible ever to be proved wrong.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel hearing 'You'll get in, you always do'?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel torn between going alone and dragging Lokesh along, and a bit sad that a friend won't give it even one try.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, certain of failing, skips an audition, so the forecast can never be tested.

passage: I'm Sahil, Keerthana's younger brother, and I only know what I saw. For two weeks she practised the monologue from the school play in front of the bathroom mirror. I could hear it through the door; it was good. Then on Thursday at dinner she said, 'I'm not going tomorrow. I'll forget the lines, everyone will see, so what's the point?' Amma asked how she knew. 'I just know.' She said it the way you'd say it's going to rain. On Friday at three, the audition time, she was on the sofa scrolling very fast. She didn't look at me. That evening a girl from her class posted the cast list. Keerthana read it for a long time and then turned the phone face down. I don't know what she was thinking. I just know she knew the lines.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana practise the monologue?
qa.a: Keerthana practised it in front of the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling as she scrolled very fast at three?
qa.a: She may have felt uneasy or regretful and been trying not to think of the audition going on without her; the forecast had felt like knowledge, but skipping left her with no answer at all.

qa.q: What choice on Thursday night could have changed the outcome?
qa.a: Keerthana could have treated 'I'll forget the lines' as a guess and gone anyway, perhaps after one run-through for Amma, since two weeks of practice was real evidence against the forecast.

qa.q: How does Sahil see what happened?
qa.a: Sahil heard the practice through the door, so he sees a sister who was ready and still stayed home, and seems quietly sad that lines he knew were good were never heard.

grounding: Shows, through a brother's eyes, a teenager who is sure she will forget her lines and skips the audition she had prepared for.

passage:
Wednesday: The notice for the inter-school dance team went up, and Nilesh tapped it. 'Saturday, 10 a.m. You're doing it, right?' Gurleen shook her head. 'They'll pick the Kathak girls from the academy. I'll be the one who loses the count. I'm not going.' She said it like reading out a timetable.
Saturday: At ten Gurleen was at home helping her mother fold laundry, not watching the clock at all, she told herself, while watching the clock.
Monday: The list was up. Nilesh had got in. So had a girl from 10C who, Nilesh said, 'lost the count twice and just laughed and kept going.' Gurleen stood in front of the notice a little longer than she needed to, reading the names again.

qa.q: When was the dance team audition?
qa.a: The audition was on Saturday at 10 a.m.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say 'I'm not going' like reading out a timetable?
qa.a: To Gurleen the failure felt like a fixed fact rather than a fear, so there seemed nothing to decide; staying away also protected her from being seen to lose the count.

qa.q: What does Monday's list show Gurleen, and what could she do with it?
qa.a: It shows that losing the count did not stop someone getting in; Gurleen could ask about the next trials and go, treating her forecast as something to test.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have hoped for when tapping the notice?
qa.a: Nilesh probably hoped Gurleen would come too and believed Gurleen had a real chance, so the flat 'I'm not going' may have been disappointing to hear.

grounding: Shows a teenager announcing she will fail the dance trials, staying home, and later seeing that a stumble did not stop others.

passage:
Trisha, you're chewing your nails over this band audition, so let your Deepika Maasi tell you something.

When I was fifteen, our school started a band. They needed a drummer. I had been drumming on every tiffin box and table in Pune for years. Everyone told me to go.

And I said, very calmly, "I'll fail." I could see it: my sticks slipping, the music teacher frowning, the older boys smirking at a girl on drums. It didn't feel like a fear. It felt like I already knew, the way you know tomorrow is Tuesday.

So I didn't go. I sat at home and polished my shoes, of all things.

Two years later, at my farewell, the music teacher said, "Why didn't you ever try for the band? We never found a decent drummer."

I never found out if I'd fail. That's the part that still pinches. The forecast was the only thing that actually stopped me.

qa.q: What did Deepika do at home instead of going to the audition?
qa.a: She sat at home and polished her shoes.

qa.q: Why did "I'll fail" feel like knowledge to fifteen-year-old Deepika?
qa.a: She could picture the whole scene so clearly, the sticks slipping and the frowns, that it felt as certain as the day of the week. Picturing it vividly made the guess feel like a fact.

qa.q: What turning point is Deepika Maasi hoping Trisha will choose differently?
qa.a: Deepika is hoping Trisha goes to the audition despite the forecast, since staying home is the only way to be sure of never finding out. Going gives the prediction a chance to be proved wrong.

qa.q: How might the music teacher's words at the farewell have felt to Deepika?
qa.a: They probably stung, showing that the chance had been real all along. Hearing the band never found a decent drummer turned the old forecast into a regret.

grounding: An aunt tells Trisha how, at fifteen, she was sure she would fail a band audition, stayed home, and so never gave the forecast a chance to be wrong.

passage:
The youth orchestra audition was at four on Saturday, across town, and it had rained since morning. Eshaan, sixteen, had exactly enough for one bus ticket each way, and the bus stand was a ten-minute walk through flooded lanes.

At two, his violin case was by the door. At two-thirty, it was still there.

Mridul called. "I'm at the stop. Where are you?"

"I'm not coming," Eshaan said. "I'll mess up the scale in the first minute. They'll stop me and say thank you. I already know how it goes. Why get soaked for that?"

"You played it perfectly on Thursday."

"Thursday doesn't count. Auditions are different."

Mridul went quiet. Then: "Okay. I'll tell you how it was."

At six, Mridul texted: "They took four violins. Only six people turned up for violin."

Eshaan read it twice and put the phone face down.

qa.q: How many people turned up for violin, according to Mridul?
qa.a: Only six people turned up for violin.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan say "Thursday doesn't count"?
qa.a: His forecast of failure feels so certain that he dismisses the evidence against it. Waving away the perfect Thursday protects the prediction and saves him from the risk of hoping.

qa.q: What choice could Eshaan have made at two-thirty, and what could he do now?
qa.a: He could have treated "I'll mess up" as a guess and gone anyway, since the audition was the only way to test it. Now he could ask whether there is a later audition or waiting list.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel waiting alone at the bus stop in the rain?
qa.a: Mridul may feel let down and a bit helpless, having seen Eshaan play well on Thursday. The careful text afterwards suggests Mridul still cares, even though Eshaan wouldn't listen.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old is sure he will fail an audition and doesn't go, so the forecast feels like knowledge and blocks any chance to disprove it.
